bracket: [Textbook misprint: two defects in this example, and the working below has been CORRECTED for the second. (1) The stem asks for "the current \(X\)", but no current labelled \(X\) appears anywhere in the figure — every branch is labelled \(I_1\) to \(I_7\), so the quantity asked for is undefined; the printed solution in fact finds \(I_3\), \(I_5\) and \(I_6\). (2) At junction C the book writes \(I_5 = I_3 + I_4\) and obtains \(I_5 = 16\) A, and hence \(I_6 = 7\) A. But in the figure the arrow on the \(I_4 = 2\) A branch points AWAY from C — drawn identically to the \(I_2 = 3\) A branch at junction B, which the same working correctly SUBTRACTS. Applying the junction law consistently with the figure gives \(I_3 = I_4 + I_5\), so \(I_5 = 14 - 2 = 12\) A and \(I_6 = 12 - 9 = 3\) A. The working below uses these corrected values.]

[Textbook misprint: the last line is printed as \(I_3 = I_1 + I_2 = 2.12 - 0.5 = 1.625\) A. The displayed subtraction is inconsistent — \(2.12 - 0.5 = 1.62\) — because \(I_1 = 2.125\) A has been truncated to 2.12 in that one line. The stated final answer \(I_3 = 1.625\) A is correct and follows from \(2.125 - 0.5\). Preserved as printed.]

[Textbook misprint: the line "Potential difference across AC \(= I_1 \times 24340 = 30\)" prints 24340, but the resistance of the arm ADC computed on the line immediately above is \(24347\ \Omega\), and the very next line correctly uses \(I_1 = 30/24347\). The 24340 is a typographical slip and the answer does not depend on it. Preserved as printed.]

[Textbook misprint: the first line of the printed solution reads "Given \(G = 25\ \mu\)A", assigning a CURRENT to the galvanometer resistance \(G\). The stem gives the resistance as \(25\ \Omega\) and the full scale deflection current as \(25\ \mu\)A, and the book's own third line correctly states \(G = 25\ \Omega\). The line has been corrected below to \(I_g = 25\ \mu\)A; the final answer is unaffected.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer is 1.66 V. The exact value is \(V = \dfrac{2}{120} \times 100 = \dfrac{5}{3} = 1.6667\) V, so to two decimal places it is 1.67 V, not 1.66 V — the book has truncated rather than rounded. The physics and the method are otherwise correct.]
